432	  \section{The machine model and elementary streams}
433	\label{sec:streams}
434	
435	A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of
436	one-dimensional tapes. A step reads and writes at most one cell on each
437	tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Fixed tracks and finitely
438	many work tapes change time by a fixed factor. We distinguish moving one
439	digit in a fixed radix, which needs a bounded number of scans, from
440	interchanging fields whose numbers of digits grow. The latter permutation
441	will be realized in Section~\ref{sec:tape-interchange} by computing XOR
442	combinations of intermediate data streams. The present section supplies
443	the elementary scans it uses. Every scan includes its counters and the
444	return of its tape heads.
445	
446	\subsection{Array order and elementary scans}
447	
448	For a positive integer $a$ write $[a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$.
449	An array with address set $[a_1]\times\cdots\times[a_t]$ is stored in
450	lexicographic order, with the first coordinate most significant.  Its
451	entries are bits unless a record width is specified.  A trailing record
452	of $B$ bits can equivalently be regarded as a final address field $[B]$.
453	An address is implicit in an entry's position in this ordered stream; it
454	is not stored beside every data bit.
455	The \emph{logical volume} $V$ is the number of stored data bits.  Work
456	tapes and duplicate streams are charged in time but do not increase $V$
457	in recurrences.  All the fields discussed below are nonempty.  A call
458	with an empty array is handled directly.
459	
460	An address permutation $f$ moves the entry at $x$ to $f(x)$.  Thus its
461	action on an array $A$ is $(fA)(f(x))=A(x)$.  Adjacent fields which are
462	irrelevant to an operation may be replaced by a single field whose length
463	is their product.  In particular, the elementary procedures below have a
464	fixed number of formal address fields even when a surrounding algorithm
465	has a growing list of coordinates.  Lengths and positions are supplied in
466	canonical binary on descriptor tapes; no additional tape head is attached to an
467	address coordinate. Each elementary call receives a fixed number of
468	collapsed canonical lengths. Constructing them from a longer surrounding
469	list is work of the caller; recursive calls below construct their own
470	collapsed descriptors within their stated bounds.
471	
472	When one address field is designated as a row field, collapse the fields
473	before it to a prefix $[P]$ and those after it to a suffix $[B]$.  If the
474	row field has range $[R]$, a \emph{row} at prefix $p$ and row index $r$
475	is the complete consecutive block $\{p\}\times\{r\}\times[B]$.
476	Every row therefore contains $B$ bits in the same suffix order.
477	
478	For headers that concatenate a list of positive integer parameters, we use
479	the self-delimiting code
480	\begin{equation}
481	 b_v=\lfloor\log_2v\rfloor+1,\qquad
482	 \Gamma(v)=0^{b_v-1}\operatorname{bin}_{b_v}(v),\qquad
483	 |\Gamma(v)|=2b_v-1\quad(v\ge1).
484	 \label{eq:integer-descriptor-code}
485	\end{equation}
486	The initial zeroes specify how many further bits follow the first one,
487	so concatenated codes can be read in order. We use this code when an
488	interface specifies a header; elementary calls still receive the fixed
489	number of canonical binary lengths described above.
490	
491	\begin{lemma}[Elementary stream operations]
492	\label{lem:elementary-streams}
493	Fix a radix $q\ge2$.  Each of the following operations on an array of
494	volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes:
495	\begin{enumerate}
496	\item any fixed permutation of the pair of digit values at two specified
497	radix-$q$ positions, whether or not the positions are adjacent;
498	\item moving one specified radix-$q$ digit to another position, preserving
499	the order of the intervening positions;
500	\item splitting on a specified radix-$q$ digit, applying a fixed
501	pointwise map to aligned streams, and merging them back;
502	\item for positive integers $P,R,B$, within each prefix of an array on
503	$[P]\times[R]\times[B]$, splitting
504	whole rows cyclically into a fixed number $W$ of streams, and, when $W$
505	divides $R$, merging those streams in any fixed order of the row classes.
506	\end{enumerate}
507	The bounds include shape preparation, counter initialization and resets,
508	and returning or clearing the visited portions of work tapes.  Their
509	constants may depend on the fixed radix, the fixed pointwise map, and the
510	fixed number of row classes.
511	\end{lemma}
512	
513	\begin{proof}
514	For the first operation split into $q^2$ streams according to the two
515	specified digits.  With these digits fixed, the order of all remaining
516	digits is unchanged by the permutation.  Enumerate output addresses in
517	their required order and read the stream prescribed by the two preimage
518	digits.  For a digit move use $q$ streams instead.  The same observation
519	shows that splitting on one digit gives streams with the same remaining
520	address set in the same order.  Scan their aligned entries, apply the
521	fixed pointwise map, and merge according to the output digit; this proves
522	the third operation.  For the fourth, write $r=Wg+w$, where
523	$0\le w<W$, and send the whole row to stream $w$.  If $W$ divides $R$,
524	each stream has address set $[P]\times[R/W]\times[B]$, indexed by the
525	prefix, $g$, and the unchanged suffix.  Thus the streams have the same
526	shape and each has volume $V/W$.  The inverse merge, with any fixed
527	permutation of the classes, reads them in the specified cyclic order.
528	
529	Here are the counter details used in these scans and later ones.  A
530	binary counter is stored with its head at the least significant end.
531	For a counter of width $w$, incrementing or decrementing and returning
532	this head over $L$ consecutive counts costs $O(L+w)$: the number of
533	visits to position $j$ is $O(1+L/2^j)$. The width term is paid when
534	initializing the counter and is absorbed by its complete range scan.  A countdown of
535	length $L$ can be initialized, reset, and tested for underflow in
536	$O(\log(2L))=O(L)$ time.  Keep a local copy of its length on a dedicated
537	track, so a reset does not search a larger descriptor.  For a nested scan
538	of a fixed number of nonempty ranges, the reset of a range is charged to
539	the scan of that range.  Induction on the number of ranges therefore gives
540	linear total counting cost.  A fixed number of empty pieces in a split
541	can be charged to the adjacent nonempty combined range.
542	
543	Only a fixed number of collapsed lengths are needed.  Computing these
544	lengths and the initial counter values by ordinary binary arithmetic
545	takes $O((\log(2V))^C)$ steps for a fixed $C$.  This is $O(V)$ uniformly
546	in $V\ge1$, after increasing a fixed constant.  Each stream is scanned a
547	fixed number of times, and every rewind, copy, or erasure is over a
548	region whose length was charged to that scan.  Delimiters and the fixed
549	number of tracks require only a fixed alphabet enlargement.
550	\end{proof}
551	
552	The next operations are linear because their target field follows their
553	control fields.  This order will be preserved whenever they are invoked.
554	
555	\begin{lemma}[Controlled shifts and fixed rational scalings]
556	\label{lem:ordered-affine-streams}
557	Fix a prime $q$, a fixed number of control fields, and finitely many
558	rational coefficients whose denominators are prime to $q$.  Whenever a
559	coefficient is used as a unit, also require its numerator to be prime to
560	$q$.  Put $Q=q^b$, $b\ge1$.
561	Suppose a target field $y\in[Q]$ follows its control fields, each control
562	used in an offset having $O(b)$ digits.  An update
563	\[
564	 y\longmapsto y+a(\text{controls})\pmod Q
565	\]
566	costs $O(V)$ if the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the
567	fixed number of control values.  In particular, this holds for a fixed
568	rational linear combination of them, specialized modulo $Q$.
569	Multiplication of $y$ by any of the specified rational units, and its
570	inverse, also costs $O(V)$.  Arbitrarily long intervening spectator
571	fields and suffix records are permitted.
572	\end{lemma}
573	
574	\begin{proof}
575	Fix all fields before the target, and let the suffix length be $B$ bits.
576	The resulting fiber consists of $Q$ consecutive blocks of length $B$.
577	For an offset $a\in[Q]$, split these blocks at $Q-a$.  Append the two
578	pieces to two tapes, doing so successively for all prefix fibers.  In the
579	merge read the second piece and then the first piece for each prefix.
580	The pieces have become the two consecutive ranges $[0,a)$ and $[a,Q)$
581	of the new target coordinate.  Recompute $a$ when starting that prefix in
582	the merge.  Initializing these two piece lengths and returning the heads
583	of the relevant control counters is included in the $b^{O(1)}$ offset
584	work.  Since
585	\[
586	 b^C=O(q^b)=O(Q)
587	\]
588	for each fixed $C$, this work is absorbed by the $QB\ge Q$ bits of the
589	fiber.  Unrelated spectator counters are incremented by ripple counting;
590	their entire contents are not consulted when computing the offset.
591	
592	For positive fixed integer $c$ prime to $q$, the permutation
593	$y\mapsto cy\pmod Q$ has $c$ increasing pieces, classified by
594	\[
595	 j=\left\lfloor\frac{cy}{Q}\right\rfloor,
596	 \qquad 0\le j<c.
597	\]
598	Prepare their endpoints once for this $Q$, split each fiber into these
599	$c$ streams, and enumerate the output coordinate $y'=0,\ldots,Q-1$.
600	The required stream is the unique $j\in[c]$ for which
601	$y'+jQ\equiv0\pmod c$.  Uniqueness follows from $\gcd(Q,c)=1$;
602	the corresponding $y=(y'+jQ)/c$ lies in $[Q]$.  The stream choice is
603	maintained by a finite residue counter.  Reversing the roles of this
604	split and merge implements multiplication by $c^{-1}$ modulo $Q$.
605	
606	Negation leaves the block at zero fixed and reverses the order of the
607	other $Q-1$ blocks.  Push these blocks consecutively to a temporary tape.
608	Popping gives their order reversed, but also reverses the bits in each
609	block.  Reverse each popped block on a second temporary tape before
610	writing it, restoring its internal order.  Every bit is moved a bounded
611	number of times.  The same procedure is repeated for successive fibers;
612	the temporary stack is emptied and its head returned locally.  A signed
613	rational unit is a composition of these integer multiplications, inverse
614	multiplications, and possibly negation.  Its description is fixed.
615	
616	The nested scan and reset analysis of
617	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams} applies to all these operations.  In
618	particular, copying a suffix-length counter at every target position
619	costs $O(\log(2B))\le O(B)$ at that position.  It does not introduce a
620	factor $\log V$ per bit.
621	\end{proof}
622	
623	When coefficients have a denominator $d$ prime to $q$, their reductions
624	modulo $q^b$ can be computed by the extended Euclidean algorithm using
625	ordinary tape arithmetic.  The dimension and all original coefficients
626	are fixed, so these preparations have polynomial cost in $b$.  Nothing
627	in Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams} assumes unit-cost arithmetic.
628	
629	For later use, fixed-width signed fixed-point binary addition,
630	subtraction, sign change, and multiplication or division by a fixed
631	power of two are streaming operations of linear bit cost, provided
632	enough integer and fractional guard bits have been allocated for exact
633	results. If an input record is most-significant-bit first, reverse it onto
634	the arithmetic work tape. With least significant bits first on that tape,
635	propagate carries using finite control. Reverse the completed record if
636	its required external order is opposite.
637	This convention separates the order of bits inside a record from the
638	lexicographic order of records. Each required reversal is a linear pass
639	and is charged.

641	\label{sec:finite-networks}
642	
643	We construct two fixed linear networks that exchange two banks of values
644	while restoring every auxiliary value.  When the values are replaced by
645	arrays, a common representation on all wires at a gate lets that gate act
646	pointwise without disturbing the representation.  We explain this invariant
647	before constructing the subspace labels that make changes of representation
648	cheap.  The first network uses bit values and rational subspaces; the second
649	uses Gaussian dyadic values and binary subspaces.  The scalar domain specifies
650	the values combined at a gate, while the subspace labels are used to construct operators
651	on each wire's address-indexed array.
652	
653	Put
654	\[
655	 h=100,\qquad v=\binom h3=161700,\qquad
656	 N=v^3=4227952113000000,\qquad m=h^3=1000000.
657	\]
658	Let $\mathcal T$ be the set of three-element subsets of $[h]$.
659	There are two data banks $X_a,Y_a$, indexed by
660	$a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in\mathcal T^3$.
661	A wire carries one scalar.  A gate is a fixed linear map on a specified
662	set of wires; untouched wires retain their values.  The vertices on a
663	wire are its source, the gates that touch it in time order, and its sink;
664	its edges join consecutive vertices.  We call the name of a wire its
665	\emph{role}, so that we can distinguish a fixed place in the network
666	from the value currently carried there.
667	
668	\subsection{Scalar operations and restored auxiliary values}
669	
670	There are three stages.  At stage $j$, fix the other two coordinates and
671	operate on the $v$ values in each bank obtained by varying coordinate $j$.  Thus
672	there are $v^2$ separate invocations at each stage.
673	Each such invocation has its own auxiliary wires, distinct from all
674	other invocations, including those in other stages.  There are
675	\[
676	 I=3v^2=78440670000
677	\]
678	invocations.  In a forward invocation, write $x_T$ for the data used as
679	controls and $y_S$ for the data to be updated; $S,T\in\mathcal T$ are
680	their varying $j$th coordinates.  These are the logical source and
681	target banks of the invocation.  For each ordered pair $(S,T)$ that is
682	neighboring under the rule below, there is an auxiliary wire $A_{ST}$.
683	There are also central wires $C_i$, $i\in[h]$, and in the second
684	construction a wire $C_\ast$.  We call all these auxiliary wires
685	\emph{scratch wires}; their initial values may be arbitrary.
686	
687	The following maps specify the construction.
688	\begin{itemize}
689	\item In the bit construction, scalars lie in $\mathbb F_2$, and
690	$S,T$ are neighbors when $|S\cap T|=1$.
691	The copy map adds $x_T$ to $A_{ST}$ for each neighbor pair.
692	The side injection adds $\sum_{T:\,|S\cap T|=1}A_{ST}$ to $y_S$.
693	The gather adds $\sum_{T\ni i}x_T$ to $C_i$, and the scatter adds
694	$\sum_{i\in S}C_i$ to $y_S$.
695	\item In the complex construction, scalars lie in
696	$\mathbb Z[i,1/2]$, and neighbors are distinct triples with even
697	intersection.  Copy is unchanged.  Side injection adds
698	\[
699	 -\sum_{T\text{ neighboring }S}\frac{|S\cap T|-1}{2}A_{ST}
700	\]
701	to $y_S$.  Gather adds $\sum_{T\ni i}x_T$ to $C_i$ and
702	$\sum_Tx_T$ to $C_\ast$.  Scatter adds
703	$(\sum_{i\in S}C_i-C_\ast)/2$ to $y_S$.
704	\end{itemize}
705	Each update leaves its control wires unchanged.  The first two rows of
706	the following schedule remove the effect of the old scratch values;
707	the next four introduce the source values and add their effect to the
708	target; the last two restore the scratch values.
709	This cancellation of arbitrary initial scratch values is a linear
710	instance of the restoration construction for transparent computation in
711	Buhrman, Cleve, Kouck\'y, Loff and Speelman~\cite[Section~3]{BuhrmanCleveKouckyLoffSpeelman2014}.
712	The forward schedule is
713	\begin{equation}
714	\begin{array}{c|l|l}
715	\text{row}&\text{operation}&\text{gate grouping}\\ \hline
716	0&\text{subtract side injection}&\text{one gate per target}\\
717	1&\text{subtract scatter}&\text{one gate on targets and center}\\
718	2&\text{copy}&\text{one gate per source}\\
719	3&\text{gather}&\text{one gate on sources and center}\\
720	4&\text{scatter}&\text{one gate on targets and center}\\
721	5&\text{side injection}&\text{one gate per target}\\
722	6&\text{undo gather}&\text{one gate on sources and center}\\
723	7&\text{undo copy}&\text{one gate per source}.
724	\end{array}
725	\label{eq:motif-schedule}
726	\end{equation}
727	
728	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:scalar-motifs}
729	For arbitrary initial values of its auxiliary wires, a forward
730	invocation changes $y_S$ to $y_S+x_S$ and leaves every other value
731	unchanged.  Performing a forward invocation from $X$ to $Y$ at stage 1,
732	the inverse forward schedule from $Y$ to $X$ at stage 2, and a forward
733	invocation from $X$ to $Y$ at stage 3 sends
734	\[
735	 (X_a,Y_a)\longmapsto(-Y_a,X_a)
736	\]
737	and restores every auxiliary value.  In the bit construction this is the
738	permutation exchanging $X_a$ and $Y_a$.
739	\end{lemma}
740	
741	\begin{proof}
742	Write $\mathcal V$ for copy, $\mathcal G$ for gather,
743	$\mathcal J$ for side injection and $\mathcal R$ for scatter.
744	If the initial side and central vectors are $a,c$, the first two rows
745	subtract $\mathcal J a+\mathcal R c$ from $y$.  Rows 2 and 3 change
746	them to $a+\mathcal Vx,c+\mathcal Gx$.  Rows 4 and 5 therefore add
747	$\mathcal R(c+\mathcal Gx)+\mathcal J(a+\mathcal Vx)$.
748	Rows 6 and 7 restore $c,a$.  The net target change is
749	$(\mathcal J\mathcal V+\mathcal R\mathcal G)x$, independently of
750	$a,c$.
751	
752	In the bit case, the central coefficient from $x_T$ to $y_S$ is
753	$|S\cap T|\bmod2$.  The side contribution cancels exactly the
754	intersection-one cases; distinct triples with intersection zero or two
755	already have coefficient zero, and the self coefficient is one.
756	In the complex case, the central coefficient is $(|S\cap T|-1)/2$.
757	The side cancels it for distinct triples with intersection zero or two;
758	intersection one contributes zero, and the self coefficient is one.
759	Thus both net maps are $y\gets y+x$.
760	
761	The inverse schedule with logical source $Y$ and target $X$ effects
762	$X\gets X-Y$.  Starting from $(x,y)$, the three stages give
763	$(x,y+x)$, then $(-y,y+x)$, then $(-y,x)$.
764	Each invocation restores its own auxiliary wires.
765	\end{proof}
766	
767	A fixed triple has
768	\[
769	 z_{\rm b}=3\binom{97}{2}=13968,\qquad
770	 z_{\rm c}=\binom{97}{3}+3\cdot97=147731
771	\]
772	neighbors in the two constructions, respectively.  The second count
773	separates intersection zero and intersection two.  Ordered pairs must
774	be counted: there are $vz$ side wires in each invocation, not $vz/2$.
775	With $c_{\rm b}=100$ and $c_{\rm c}=101$ central wires per invocation,
776	the total wire counts are
777	\begin{align}
778	 W_{\rm b}&=2N+I(vz_{\rm b}+c_{\rm b})
779	          =177176569091445000000,\label{eq:bit-wire-count}\\
780	 W_{\rm c}&=2N+I(vz_{\rm c}+c_{\rm c})
781	          =1873807244643542670000.\label{eq:complex-wire-count}
782	\end{align}
783	All these numbers are fixed, independently of any eventual input length.
784	
785	\subsection{From scalar values to arrays}
786	
787	We record the representation principle before choosing the labels.  Let
788	$R$ be the scalar ring of either network and let $\Omega$ be a finite address
789	set common to all wires.  Replace each scalar by an array in $R^\Omega$, and
790	apply each scalar gate pointwise at every address.  Write $\mathsf S_\Omega$
791	for the resulting network on the vector of wire arrays.
792	
793	At each source, gate and sink $v$, assign an invertible $R$-linear operator
794	$D_v$ on $R^\Omega$, called its \emph{frame}.  A frame acts on the values
795	indexed by addresses within one wire's array and may mix them; a gate instead
796	combines wire values at each fixed address.  All incoming and outgoing
797	incidences of one gate use the same $D_v$.  On an edge from $u$ to $v$, apply
798	$D_vD_u^{-1}$ to that wire's array.  Define the operators on all input and
799	output roles by
800	\[
801	 D_{\rm in}=\bigoplus_w D_{\mathrm{source}(w)},\qquad
802	 D_{\rm out}=\bigoplus_w D_{\mathrm{sink}(w)}.
803	\]
804	For a supplied physical input $f$, define its logical interpretation to be
805	$g=D_{\rm in}^{-1}f$; this definition requires no physical preprocessing.
806	At a vertex $v$, the invariant is that the stored array equals $D_v$ applied
807	to the logical array there.  It holds at the sources by definition.  On an
808	edge whose logical array is $\varphi$, the edge operator changes $D_u\varphi$
809	to $D_v\varphi$.  At a gate with logical input arrays $\varphi_j$,
810	$R$-linearity gives
811	$\sum_j c_jD_v\varphi_j=D_v(\sum_j c_j\varphi_j)$ for each output combination, with
812	$c_j\in R$.  Thus the common frame commutes with the pointwise gate, and
813	the invariant continues to the sinks.  The implemented operator is therefore
814	\begin{equation}
815	 D_{\rm out}\,\mathsf S_\Omega\,D_{\rm in}^{-1}.
816	 \label{eq:common-frame-identity}
817	\end{equation}
818	In particular, if the scalar network is a signed role permutation that
819	sends input role $w$ to output role $\rho(w)$ with scalar sign
820	$\varepsilon_w$, that route applies
821	$\varepsilon_wD_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}
822	D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$ to its input array.  All roles, including
823	the auxiliary roles, enter this identity.  Once the scalar routing is fixed,
824	the endpoint frames determine the array operator on each route; the
825	intermediate frames can then be chosen to make each edge change inexpensive.
826

832	$D_u g_w\ \xrightarrow{\quad D_vD_u^{-1}\quad}\ D_v g_w$\\
833	the frame changes while the logical array stays fixed};
834	\node[box,below=of c] (d) {One pointwise gate $G$ on $t$ aligned roles, all in frame $D_v$\\
835	$G(D_vg_1,\ldots,D_vg_t)=D_vG(g_1,\ldots,g_t)$};
836	\draw[->] (c)--(d);
837	\end{tikzpicture}
838	 \caption{An edge changes the representation of one role's logical array
839	$g_w$. At the next gate $G$, all $t$ input arrays have the common frame
840	$D_v$, so the pointwise linear gate commutes with that frame. The same
841	$D_v$ acts on each output component.}
842	\label{fig:frame-compatibility}
843	\end{figure}
844	
845	\subsection{Subspaces attached to the gates}
846	
847	The scalar network already has the required signed exchange. We now
848	choose its intermediate labels to make the changes of frame inexpensive.
849	A label is a nondegenerate subspace of a fixed bilinear space. On every
850	edge one label will contain the other. For such an edge, the
851	\emph{orthogonal residual} is the orthogonal complement of the smaller label inside
852	the larger one; its dimension is the absolute change in label dimension.
853	The saving will come from keeping the total dimension lost on decreasing
854	edges small relative to $N$.
855	
856	For the bit network, let $F=\mathbb Q^h$ with bilinear form
857	\[
858	 \langle x,y\rangle=x^{\mathsf T}(I-J/9)y,
859	\]
860	where $J$ is the all-one matrix.  This form has eigenvalues $1$ and
861	$1-h/9=-91/9$, so it is nondegenerate.  For a triple $T$ let $t_T$ be
862	its indicator vector.  Then
863	\[
864	 \langle t_S,t_T\rangle=|S\cap T|-1,
865	 \qquad \langle t_T,t_T\rangle=2.
866	\]
867	For the complex network, take instead $F=\mathbb F_2^h$ with the
868	ordinary dot product; here $t_T\cdot t_T=1$.
869	Thus every triple line is nondegenerate, and neighboring triple lines
870	are orthogonal, in the label field belonging to either construction.
871	The scalar domain need not equal the label field.
872	These degree-one intersection formulas specialize the construction
873	described by Alon~\cite[Section~3, remark after Theorem~1.1]{Alon1998}
874	to the prime $2$, with the ground-set size changed to $h=100$.
875	
876	The ambient label space is $\mathcal F=F^{\otimes3}$ with its tensor
877	bilinear form.  It has dimension $m$ and is nondegenerate.  Write
878	\[
879	 u_a=t_{a_1}\otimes t_{a_2}\otimes t_{a_3},\qquad U_a=\langle u_a\rangle.
880	\]
881	The prescribed terminal labels are
882	\[
883	\begin{array}{c|cc}
884	\text{role}&\text{source label}&\text{sink label}\\ \hline
885	X_a&U_a&\mathcal F\\
886	Y_a&0&U_a^\perp\\
